description: We are LUMEN (Lunar Uncertainty & Multiresolution Elevation Navigator), a team of Brazilian STEAM students driven by a passion for space exploration, technology, programming, and artificial intelligence. Our team is made up of Larissa, Eduardo, and Luiz.
summary:
LUMEN is a browser-based mission cockpit that lets anyone pick a landing site and a date at the lunar South Pole and immediately see where the Sun and the Earth sit relative to the real terrain horizon. It answers the operational questions that matter: how long until sunset and earthset, how much solar power the rover gets, when direct-to-Earth communication is possible, and what happens if the landing slips by a lunar day or moves to a nearby site.

Users choose a rover, filter 130 Artemis candidate sites through a viability funnel, land on a 3D LOLA surface, and compare Plan A against Plan B side by side. An Engineer Mode exports the horizon mask and Sun/Earth data as CSV.

Our key contribution is a multiresolution safety layer: published site catalogs use 60 m grids, but rovers face 5 m hazards. LUMEN uses real 5 m LOLA data to show the hazards coarse grids hide and applies calibrated safety margins (P50/P90/P99).

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive tool for exploring how lunar terrain affects sunlight and visibility of Earth at a selected location. It helps you investigate potential landing sites and observation windows, understand when solar power and direct-to-Earth communication may be available, and identify the terrain responsible for blocking the Sun or Earth. Explore the interface through three complementary views, moving from the whole Moon to the horizon at your chosen site.

1. Explore the Moon — global view: Use the interactive globe to locate regions and landing-site markers within the broader lunar landscape. Rotate the Moon to explore different areas and establish your geographical context.

2. South Pole in detail — regional view: Switch to the polar map to examine candidate landing regions and select individual sites. Click a region to explore its sites, or double-click a point to investigate custom coordinates. These views help you answer two different questions: Where on the Moon am I looking? and Which specific location do I want to investigate?

3. From the ground — local view: Explore the terrain around your selected site and see the Sun and Earth relative to its horizon. Drag to look around, then play, pause or move along the timeline to inspect changing conditions. Select an obstruction explanation to locate the terrain feature blocking the Sun or Earth. This view answers: What would an observer at this location see, and what obstructs the view?

To configure your analysis, choose the start date, observation duration and observer height. Review sunlight availability, Earth visibility, time with both visible, and the longest periods of continuous light and darkness. Compare terrain resolutions to understand how map detail changes predictions, or explore the annual summary to find favorable windows. Change locations and dates to compare scenarios, switch between English and Portuguese, and share a link to your selection. Consult the validation information when interpreting results: these tools support exploration and preliminary assessment, while the associated LUMEN research separately investigates how sparse laser measurements and topographic uncertainty can improve terrain-hazard assessment and rover navigation.



WHAT IT DOES

LUMEN guides the user through three screens: (1) choose a rover, mission year, duration and communication mode (direct to Earth or relay); (2) explore a real Moon map (globe and South Pole 3D view built from LOLA elevation) where 130 candidate sites are filtered by a viability funnel; (3) land and watch the Sun and Earth move along a 360° horizon mask computed from terrain, with live countdowns to sunset and earthset, battery, solar array output and Earth link status.

A "Plan A × Plan B" comparator answers the rescheduling question directly: same site on the next lunar day, a one-year delay, or a neighboring site. A mission forecast reports solar visibility, mean illumination, Earth visibility, worst blackout and minimum battery.

Users can pick among real rovers and, as an educational "what if", Mars rovers placed on the Moon. Each rover's battery, solar array, mast height and slope limit change which sites survive the funnel; estimated values are flagged in the app.

WHAT IS NEW

Only 7.29% of the 5 m pixels in the 87.5–90°S LOLA grid contain a real laser shot; the rest are interpolated. Site catalogs are computed at 60 m, where small craters and slopes disappear. Our 10×10 km Inspector overlays what the 60 m and 20 m grids hide, marks real LOLA shots, and applies P50/P90/P99 safety margins. In the tactical 5 m driving mode, an A* planner and a 100-rover evolutionary swarm compare a route planned on the 60 m grid with one planned on the multiresolution map.

Contribution at a glance

LUMEN combines 60 m or 20 m maps with elevation residuals derived from actual LOLA laser measurements to produce a local correction at the 5 m scale. By incorporating measurement density into uncertainty margins and route planning, it reduces unvetoed hazards and improves rover arrival under the tested conditions.

The central contribution is to use measured data more effectively when deciding where to travel, with explicit uncertainty and physical protection.

This summary focuses on results attributable to LUMEN. Illumination validation and auxiliary modules are mentioned only where needed to define the scope of the central contribution.

 

1 | The problem that makes LUMEN relevant

Route planning at the lunar south pole requires assessing local slopes, crater rims and narrow passages. Maps at 60 m or 20 m lose local detail; nominal 5 m maps may contain extensive interpolated areas. The thesis addresses this mismatch between pixel size and physical measurement coverage.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 2. Direct LOLA coverage across grid scales in the 87.5°S–90°S cap. Redrawn from source Section 3.2; the 120 m value is reported in Section 1.2.

In the 87.5°S–90°S cap, direct coverage rises from 7.29% of cells at 5 m to 67.97% at 20 m and 99.40% at 60 m. These percentages indicate at least one shot per cell; they do not imply that all detail within a larger cell is known.

Of the 130 catalog sites, 104 have a nominal 5 m product and 26 do not. Those 26 points are distinct from the 26 blocks used in the Monte Carlo analysis. Application outside fine-map coverage is relevant, but the reported tests used blocks where the fine reference exists.

Scientific relevance: make observational density part of the safety decision.

Source: report Sections 1.2–1.4 and 3.1–3.3.

 

2 | The thesis and its mechanism

The correction spreads only around measured shots and decays to zero away from them. The method therefore preserves the base where observations are missing, without generating unsupported terrain detail. Estimated slope plus an uncertainty margin determines whether a segment exceeds the 15° limit; sensors and replanning update decisions during the traverse.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 3. LUMEN conceptual workflow based on the source methodology.

From observations to a local correction

• Prepare the base: smoothly resample the 60 m or 20 m grid onto the 5 m working mesh.

• Measure the residual: at shot locations, compute the difference between observed elevation and the base.

• Fuse with bounded support: spread residuals within the neighborhood, preserve measured values and reduce their influence with distance.

• Turn uncertainty into decisions: vary the margin with local confidence and avoid slopes incompatible with the 15° limit.

Margins and control work together

In the nominal dynamic battery, LUMEN uses a +2.0° margin at shots and +3.6° elsewhere. Planning uses eight-neighbor Dijkstra search; sensors support a reaction near 14.5° and replanning when the rover becomes blocked. Protection must be updated using local observations so that uncertainty does not always lead to immobilization.

P50, P90 and P99 denote probabilistic margin levels under the adopted model, rather than absolute safety guarantees. The central gain summarized here concerns LUMEN with P90, compared with the controls specified for each experiment.

Source: report Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.4 and 5.5.

Separating tuning from testing

For navigation, 52 corridors of 3 km × 550 m were extracted: 34 for tuning, 2 for validation and 16 for final testing. Each strategy and scenario involves 1,600 traverses. The statistically independent unit used in the report is the corridor, rather than each rover within a strip.

The most important control

In Monte Carlo, the conventional grid's uniform margin is adjusted by bisection to reproduce LUMEN's false alarm, with a reported maximum difference of 0.02 percentage point. This isolates the added value of spatially combining measurements and using a density-based margin beyond simply increasing caution everywhere.

Reading the indicators

• Unvetoed real hazard: the hazard indicator remaining after the blocking rule is applied; lower values are better.

• False alarm: blocking terrain classified as safe by the reference; it must be controlled for a fair comparison.

• Arrival and tip-over: distinct simulation outcomes. More arrivals do not automatically imply fewer tip-overs in every scenario.

Source: Sections 3.3–3.5, 4.2, 5.2, 5.3.2 and 5.5. Values summarize the report's tables; raw data were not reprocessed for this summary.

 

4 | Central evidence: beyond the margin alone

The largest initial protection gain comes from incorporating uncertainty. On the 60 m grid, adding a margin reduces median unvetoed hazard from 28.7% to 6.45%. LUMEN adds a second gain: at equivalent false alarm, the value falls to 3.88%.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 1. Source Table 04. Only the last two bars have equalized false alarm, with a median of approximately 17.9%.

Improvement at 26 of 26 sites  •  Paired Wilcoxon: p = 3 × 10⁻⁸

The reported 38.5% reduction summarizes reductions across sites, with an interquartile range of 32%–44%. Because medians are computed separately, the ratio between 6.45% and 3.88% does not necessarily reproduce that summary. Values are retained as reported in the source.

Median slope error also decreases, from 1.08° for the 60 m grid to 0.61° for nominal LUMEN. The report associates larger gains with rougher terrain, with a correlation of 0.91.

Why this is the strongest result

It combines replication across multiple sites, paired comparison and control of the false-alarm cost. It directly supports the conclusion that measured residuals add useful information to the protection rule.

Source: Section 5.2, Table 04. The calibrated variant reaches 3.44%, but at higher false alarm (19.2%); it is therefore not presented as an improvement at equal cost.

 

5 | Robustness and the 20 m starting grid

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 2. Curves redrawn from the six points in source Table 05. Lines connect published values; they do not represent new experiments.

LUMEN's advantage appears across the tested range: the reported median reduction across sites increases from 29% to 42% as false alarm rises from 5% to 30%. The result is not restricted to the nominal 17.9% operating point.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 3. Equal-false-alarm comparison for the 20 m base. Source: Table 04; the aggregate false-alarm value for this comparison is not provided in that table.

Starting from 20 m, unvetoed hazard falls from 3.57% to 3.19%. The reported gain is 12% (interquartile range: 7%–16%), with improvement at 24/26 sites and p = 7.5 × 10⁻⁷. Median slope error decreases from 0.55° to 0.47°.

The incremental benefit is smaller because the base already contains more detail. At 3.88%, the 60→5 m version does not fully replace the protected 20 m grid, at 3.57%, in this static test. The positive finding is that the method adds value to both bases while remaining sensitive to initial data quality.

 

6 | Navigation: more successful arrivals

Dynamic evaluation brings the analysis closer to operational decisions: the rover must make progress, react to terrain and replan. Unlike static Monte Carlo, LUMEN versus R60 combines map and margin differences; it does not isolate reconstruction alone.

The advantage over the 60 m grid retains its direction at the 800 s limit. The 4,000 s limit is an extended window, not an unlimited simulation. Difficult scenarios use amplified relief and do not include a moving shadow cycle.

 

7 | Dynamic safety and statistical evidence

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 5. Tip-overs in N1 and N2 with a 4,000 s limit. Source: Tables 09b–09c.

In N1 and N2, more arrivals are accompanied by fewer tip-overs: 10.6% falls to 8.0%, and 11.2% to 8.6%. This reduction is not universal: in N0 and N3, LUMEN has a slightly higher tip-over rate than R60.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 6. Paired gains and bootstrap 95% CIs (5,000 resamples); p-values from Wilcoxon tests per corridor. Source: Table 10. These are different statistical procedures.

The paired evidence per corridor is significant in N1 (p = 0.027), but not in N0 or N2 at the 5% level. The report did not correct for multiple comparisons in this battery. Per-rover tests are indicative because the 100 traverses within each corridor share the same terrain.

In N1/N2, LUMEN's arrival rate does not differ significantly from the unmarginated 5 m “oracle.” This does not establish equivalence: the oracle uses an exact map without an uncertainty margin and is not a guaranteed performance ceiling.

 

8 | Ablation: what drives the improvement

The ablation compares successive configurations on 30 unseen synthetic terrains, with 60 rovers per terrain. It aims to distinguish the contribution of the multiresolution map from that of locking and additional optimization modules.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 7. Mean arrival by configuration. Source: Table 07a. Synthetic terrains; these percentages are not directly comparable with the LOLA battery.

Introducing LUMEN: 56.3% → 95.2% arrival (+38.9 pp)

D2 versus D1c is significant per terrain using paired Wilcoxon with Holm correction (p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁵). The C2r control retains 95.2% without continuous adjustment, reinforcing that this module does not explain the main result. Selection of the best route rises from 5/30 to 20/30 terrains.

Simplex does not change arrival at the step where it is introduced. Subsequent evolutionary tuning reaches 95.9%, without a significant gain over the thesis configuration. MLP and hybrid networks yield 90.9% and 82.1%; their decreases are not significant per terrain, although they are significant in the per-rover analysis.

A strength is the sufficiency of an interpretable deterministic architecture in the tests performed. This comparison, restricted to small networks, does not support a general conclusion about artificial intelligence.

 

9 | The spatial reach of the benefit

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 4. Failures in NPC and Haworth. Panels from source Figure 21 with English labels. The diagnosis relates residual errors to slope and terrain structure. The bottom legend strip of each source panel is omitted; the visible terrain is unchanged.

The report locates many residual errors near the 15° threshold, often on slopes of 15°–17°. This suggests that local margin adjustments may be more useful than increasing protection everywhere. The tested +1° reinforcement reduces failures on rough terrain but adds false alarms in flat areas.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Chart 8. Haworth: 3.3 million cells without shots, SfS reference and 20% false alarm. Source: Section 5.3.2.

LUMEN does not outperform the 60 m map in this no-shot subset and trails the official 5 m product. This bounds the contribution: use nearby observational support without claiming to recover unknown detail between tracks. Where available, the official 5 m map remains preferable.

 

10 | Strengths and practical relevance

1. A measurable, verifiable contribution

The thesis connects a simple physical rule—correct from existing measurements—to quantified safety outcomes. Equal false alarm demonstrates added information, while replication at 26 sites reduces dependence on a favorable example.

2. Connecting maps, uncertainty and action

LUMEN extends beyond terrain reconstruction: shot density guides margins used in route planning. Dynamic tests show that the combination can improve arrival and reduce tip-overs in N1/N2 when local sensing and replanning remain available.

3. A transparent architecture

Observed residuals, explicit margins and geometric decisions make outcomes inspectable. Ablation helps prioritize the components that deliver benefit: multiresolution mapping, physical protection and active navigation. Auxiliary modules need not be credited with the central gain.

4. Compatibility with multiple data scales

The 60→5 m and 20→5 m variants adapt the contribution to the available base. In the dynamic battery, RT20 adds +4.1 and +7.4 percentage points over the margin-protected 20 m grid in N1 and N2 (paired differences from Table 10), without significance per corridor at 5%.

5. Identified limits support appropriate use

Haworth reveals where refinement loses its advantage, while N3 exposes the cost of closing passages without replanning. These findings help define application requirements: support from nearby measurements, active sensors and adjustment of margins.

LUMEN's relevance lies in combining demonstrated gains with explicit conditions of use.

Potential application: support route decisions where only a coarse base and local observations are available. This transfer requires targeted validation outside the fine-map blocks used in the experiments.

 

11 | Conclusion and evidence traceability

The evidence supports LUMEN as the thesis's central contribution: multiresolution fusion guided by real shots, coupled with uncertainty margins, improves hazard detection at equal false alarm and benefits simulated navigation under defined conditions. The strongest result is the 38.5% static gain across 26 sites; the main operational complement is up to +14.4 percentage points in arrival, with fewer tip-overs in N1/N2.

Conditions attached to this conclusion

• The 60 m and 20 m bases were aggregated from fine maps; transfer to regions genuinely lacking a 5 m product has not been tested directly.

• Sparse shots and interpolated neighbors limit the slope reference. Static Monte Carlo draws errors point by point; the dynamic simulator smooths errors spatially.

• The expected processing reduction was not measured in runtime, memory or map volume.

• The 486 photographs and illumination tests did not evaluate the LUMEN reconstruction; they are not used here as evidence of its performance.

• P50/P90/P99 margins against SfS were evaluated on official 5 m LOLA, without equalizing false alarm. Those results are not attributed to LUMEN.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML/CSS and Three.js (WebGL) for the app, which runs entirely in the browser with no backend. Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, SpiceyPy, tifffile, Pillow) and C for precomputation and validation. TypeScript and Node.js for the mission core and automated tests.

USE OF AI

AI tools (Claude, Gemini, OpenClaw) assisted with code, data-processing scripts and documentation. AI-assisted elements are identified in the repository.
